title: Why he wept (Berakhot 28b)
hookLine: Yochanan ben Zakkai weeps at death, not knowing which road he'll be led on
tomorrow: the same prayer, every day. how does it not go stale?

cards: The students come in quietly, the way people walk into a hospital room. Their teacher, Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, is near the end of his life. When he sees them, he begins to cry.
They don't know what to do with that. Lamp of Israel, they say. Right-hand pillar.
Mighty hammer. Why are you weeping?

teach.b: His answer comes in two parts.

First: if I were being led before a human king, who is here today and in the grave tomorrow, whose anger doesn't last forever, whom I could calm with words or even bribe with money, even then I would weep.
Now I'm being led before the King of kings, who lives forever. Then the part that stops the room.

teach.h: TWO ROADS, AND I DON'T KNOW.
teach.b: There are two roads before me, he says, one to the Garden of Eden and one to Gehinnom, and I don't know on which one they'll lead me. Shall I not weep? Here's what to tell a friend tonight.
The teacher his students called the lamp of Israel didn't pretend to know. He said it in front of them: I don't know, and I'm afraid. The Talmud keeps that in.
It doesn't tidy his faith into calm.

teach.h: FEAR OF HEAVEN, LIKE FEAR OF PEOPLE.
teach.b: Then they ask him for a blessing, and he gives a surprising one: may your fear of heaven be like your fear of people.
If only, he says. When someone does wrong, they think, just let nobody see me. And at the very end, his words turn toward a guest: prepare a chair for Hezekiah, king of Judah, who is coming.

how: Jewish tradition does not ask the dying or the frightened to hide fear; visiting the sick (bikkur cholim) and sitting with them honestly is counted as a mitzvah.

o: a great teacher weeps because he honestly doesn't know
a teacher cries because his students forgot his lessons
a sage mourns the Temple on the day it was destroyed

games.q: in the room — tap the pairs.
p: fear heaven as you fear people

s: a person of deep faith shouldn't be afraid of what comes next
Yochanan ben Zakkai, the lamp of Israel, wept and said: I don't know.
his last blessing: may your fear of heaven be like your fear of people
when people do wrong, he says, they think: let nobody see me.
the Talmud leaves out the teacher's tears to protect his name
it tells them plainly, with his reason.

games.q: you're one of the students. your teacher, the one everyone looks to, is weeping. what do you do?
o: ask him why, and stay to hear the answer.
tell him a man like him has nothing to fear.
step out quietly so he can cry alone.
games.why: they asked, 'why are you weeping?' and he told them the truth: two roads, and I don't know which. then they asked for a blessing.

practice: Close your eyes and let one thing you honestly don't know come to mind: about health, someone you love, or what's next. Don't solve it or argue with it.
Let it sit beside you, the way the students sat beside their teacher, and breathe with it.

wordCard.voice: Why he wept. Yochanan ben Zakkai, near death: two roads before me, and I don't know which. Honest fear, inside a life of faith.

orig.note: Hebrew: and I don't know. Yochanan ben Zakkai on which road he'll be led.

carryVoice: Your line: even he wept. Not knowing, said out loud, by the lamp of Israel. Nineteen of fifty.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Berakhot 28b (Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai weeps before his students; two roads; the blessing of fear of heaven; prepare a chair for Hezekiah)
